_note: READER-FACING DOCUMENTS AND WHAT EACH ONE DESCRIBES.
practice: change-updates-its-docs. A change to a mechanism is supposed
to update the document that describes that mechanism in the SAME
commit. This registry is what makes the omission findable afterwards:
very_deep_check.py compares each document's last commit against the
last commit touching anything in its `describes` list, and reports the
ones the world moved out from under.
It is a REVIEW list, never a gate. A document can legitimately be older
than the code it describes -- the change may not have altered anything
a reader sees. No script can tell those apart, which is exactly why the
finding is printed for a person instead of failing a build
(practice: fail-gracefully).
`describes` holds paths, not globs: a file or a directory, matched by
git log the same way either way. Keep each list SHORT and specific --
a list that names half the repository reports every document as stale
every run, which is the same as reporting nothing.
`must_mention` is the other half, and it is the tighter one: a phrase a
person is expected to SAY has to appear, literally, in the document
they would learn it from. Nothing else in the tree checks that a
feature reached a human at all.

documentation/DAILY_HABITS.md.why: It teaches the standing command vocabulary. A command whose meaning changes, or a new one landing, changes what this page has to say.

documentation/FOR_EVERYONE_ELSE.md.why: It walks a non-developer through how an idea becomes a rule, who approves it, and how a rule moves between levels.

documentation/FOR_DEVELOPERS.md.why: It is the developer-facing account of the four loader channels and the enforced channel, plus the commands that read them.

documentation/WHY_PRECEDENT.md.why: It is the pitch. It goes stale when the project's own account of what it is changes.

INSTALL.md.why: It is the step-by-step install, and every step of it names a template, a tool invocation, or a config key.

SETUP.md.why: It is the conversational front door to the same install, so it drifts from INSTALL.md's mechanics rather than from the code directly.

documentation/INSTALL.md.why: It is a one-paragraph signpost: it tells a reader arriving in documentation/ that the install steps live at the repository root and that SETUP.md drives the same steps conversationally. It carries no instructions of its own, so it goes stale only when one of those two moves or is renamed -- which is exactly what nothing else would catch.

documentation/ADOPTING.md.why: It explains the three-source model to someone deciding whether to adopt it; the source model changing is what dates it.

documentation/GITHUB_SETTINGS.md.why: It is the one-page account of every GitHub setting Precedent depends on: roles, branch protection, CODEOWNERS and the tokens. A change to how CODEOWNERS is generated, which paths a project owns, or which token a workflow needs is what dates it.

documentation/TEN_THINGS.md.why: It is the ten-point summary of how the system works, each point linking into a longer document. It goes stale when any of those documents changes its account of the mechanism it points at.

spoken-commands.rule: Every active practice whose `defines:` list carries a phrase beginning with a capital letter is a phrase a PERSON says out loud. It has to appear, verbatim, in the document that claims to teach the vocabulary.
spoken-commands.why: A command nobody was told about is a command nobody uses. This is the one mechanical answer to 'is the feature documented where a human reads?' -- the rest of that question needs a person, and gets one every very deep check.
spoken-commands.story: Raised by Morgan 2026-09-08, in the same message that asked for the day-to-day guide: 'this should also check to make sure the features that are important for humans to know are documented.'
